title: Air India Crash Probe in Final Stage, Government Tells Supreme Court
excerpt: Solicitor General Tushar Mehta sought two to three weeks to finish the AI171 investigation as the court weighs petitions for an independent probe.
body:
• The investigation into the June 2025 Air India crash that killed 260 people is in its final stage, the government told the Supreme Court on Wednesday.
  • Solicitor General Tushar Mehta asked for two to three weeks to complete the process, and the bench agreed to adjourn.
  • The court is hearing petitions, including one by the captain's father, seeking a separate independent investigation.
  • The July 2025 preliminary report found the Boeing 787's engine fuel-control switches moved from "run" to "cutoff" seconds after take-off; it did not establish why.

The investigation into last year's Air India crash, which killed 260 people, is in its final stage, the Indian government told the Supreme Court on Wednesday, Reuters reported.

"We are at the fag end (of the investigation). We have to follow global protocols. There is no reason why we should delay deliberately."

— Tushar Mehta, Solicitor General of India

Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Centre and the Directorate General of Civil Aviation, asked the bench — Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana — to adjourn the case for two to three weeks, and the bench agreed, according to Law Finder News. Advocate Prashant Bhushan, for the petitioners, pointed out that the final report had still not been made public and sought an early hearing.

Why the case is in court

The court is hearing petitions seeking an independent, court-monitored investigation into the crash, including one filed by Pushkar Raj Sabharwal, father of the flight's captain, Sumeet Sabharwal, and another by the NGO Safety Matters Foundation. Pushkar Raj Sabharwal has criticised investigators, saying officials from India's Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) implied, during a visit to his home, that his son had cut the fuel supply to the plane's engines, Reuters reported. The court has said it will await the final AAIB report before deciding the petitions.

What the investigation has found so far

Air India flight AI171, a Boeing 787-8 flying from Ahmedabad to London Gatwick on June 12, 2025, crashed shortly after take-off, killing 241 of the 242 people on board and 19 people on the ground. The aircraft was flown by Captain Sumeet Sabharwal with co-pilot Captain Clive Kunder.

A preliminary report released in July 2025 found that the aircraft's engine fuel-control switches had moved from the "run" to the "cutoff" position seconds after take-off, starving both engines of fuel. It did not establish why the switches had moved. The report said one pilot was heard asking the other why he had cut off the fuel, and the other denied doing so; investigators did not identify which pilot made either remark.

The AAIB told the court in July 2026 that it had prepared a cockpit voice recorder transcript and conducted a psychological autopsy as part of its investigation. At the time, it expected a draft final report around October, to be circulated to participating countries for comments before being finalised and published. The bureau has also told the court there is a statutory prohibition on disclosing cockpit voice recordings to any external committee or the public.

What happens next

On the government's own timeline, the remaining work takes two to three weeks. Families of the 260 victims have now waited more than 17 months since the crash for the final report, which is the document that will assign findings on what moved the fuel switches — and the Supreme Court's decision on whether a separate independent investigation is needed will follow it.
